name: Canthal tilt theory

card.summary: The idea that the upward or downward angle of the eye corners drives how attractive a face is; the angle is real and measurable, the strong rule built on it is not well studied.
card.aka: Canthal tilt, positive/negative canthal tilt, NCT/PCT
card.note: Surgical and DIY 'fixes' discussed online carry the usual risks of eyelid and orbital procedures; no trial tests the attractiveness rule itself.

quick.overview:
Canthal tilt is the angle of the line joining the inner and outer corners of the eye relative to horizontal. In looksmaxxing communities a 'positive' tilt (outer corner higher than the inner) is treated as a mark of an attractive, masculine or 'predatory' look, while a 'negative' tilt (outer corner lower) is treated as a handicap.

Surgeons and anthropometry researchers measure canthal tilt as a routine photographic landmark, and average values have been reported for some groups. The stronger claim, that tilt is a primary driver of attractiveness, has little direct published testing, and forum threads mostly debate whether it can be changed.
quick.mechanism: Tilt is determined by the position of the eye corners (canthi), which are anchored by the lateral and medial canthal tendons and the shape of the bony orbit. Forum users argue that cheekbone and upper-jaw support changes it; surgeons describe procedures such as canthoplasty that alter the outer corner. Makeup and lash styling can change how tilt appears without altering anatomy.
quick.risks: Measuring tilt carries no risk. Procedures people discuss to change it (canthopexy or canthoplasty, filler, orbital or midface surgery) are medical procedures with the ordinary surgical risks, and some forum threads describe do-it-yourself approaches that clinicians would not endorse. Community discussion also links the concept with distress for some users who describe a negative tilt as decisive.

lead: Canthal tilt is the angle between a horizontal line and the line joining the inner corner (medial canthus) and outer corner (lateral canthus) of the eye.[2][4] In looksmaxxing slang a positive tilt means the outer corner sits higher than the inner corner, a neutral tilt means they are level, and a negative tilt means the outer corner sits lower.[1][10]

The canthal tilt theory is the community belief that this angle is a major determinant of facial attractiveness, especially in men, and that a positive tilt signals a dominant or masculine look, often paired with the term 'hunter eyes'.[1][10] Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists canthal tilt among the core terms of the subculture.[10]

Outside the community, canthal tilt appears as a measurement in plastic surgery and craniofacial research, for example in studies of eyelid surgery, facial feminization surgery and congenital skull-shape correction.[4][6][11] Studies of beauty-pageant winners and of attractiveness have reported tilt values or examined it as a cue, but no large trial has established it as a principal driver of attractiveness.[3][5]

paras: The canthi are the two corners where the upper and lower eyelids meet. The outer corner is sharper and the lids lie close to the eyeball there, while the inner corner extends toward the nose.[2] The line connecting the two canthi is the palpebral fissure axis, and its angle from horizontal is the canthal tilt.[2][4]

In East Asian and some Southeast Asian people the epicanthal fold often covers the inner corner, which can change how tilt is judged by eye. Surgical papers on epicanthoplasty address how that region interacts with the look of the upper eyelid.[2][7]

Researchers usually measure tilt from standardized photographs or 3D images. A 2024 cross-sectional study of 145 patients with dermatochalasis used 3D photogrammetry to record canthal tilt alongside other eyelid dimensions and compared values by age and sex.[4] A study of 21 beauty-pageant winners reported a mean canthal tilt of about 9 degrees (plus or minus 2).[3]
Because measures depend on head position, lighting and which landmarks are used, values from different studies are not always directly comparable.

The term came into wide use in the online looksmaxxing and incel-adjacent forums of the 2010s alongside the PSL rating scale and vocabulary such as mogging and hunter eyes, and later spread through video platforms.[1][10]
Looksmax.org contains many threads devoted to the topic, for example asking whether tilt can be raised, whether a negative tilt is disqualifying, or how to correct asymmetry.[9][8]
No studies found that test canthal tilt theory itself, meaning a trial showing that tilt alone determines attractiveness or that a given intervention improves ratings of attractiveness.

Related research uses canthal tilt as an outcome measure in surgery. In a 2023 comparison of two operations for unilateral coronal craniosynostosis, distraction patients showed significantly better postoperative symmetry in canthal tilt than a matched cohort treated with advancement and remodeling.[6] A 2024 comparison of endoscopic-assisted and open distraction also tracked canthal tilt symmetry.[14] A 2007 ophthalmic plastic surgery paper asked whether medial canthal tilt is a powerful cue for facial attractiveness.[5] A review of facial feminization surgery noted that patients undergoing brow lift and eyelid surgery had a higher rate of negative canthal tilt at baseline.[11]

sections.h: Methods people discuss for changing tilt
paras: General categories mentioned in community threads include makeup and eyeliner, lash trimming, exercises, 'mewing', bone-smashing, and surgery such as canthoplasty or canthopexy.[8][9][13] A cosmetic surgery literature on lateral canthoplasty describes the procedure mainly to correct or prevent lower eyelid malposition, with outcomes studied in retrospective series.[12]
No controlled study has shown that mewing or facial exercises change canthal tilt.

Users post photos for tilt assessment, argue over whether tilt is mainly bone-structure or soft-tissue, and sometimes describe a negative tilt as a serious disadvantage. Others in the same forums argue the concept is overweighted or that eye-area appeal depends on other traits.[8][9]

timeline.event: A paper in Ophthalmic Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery asks whether medial canthal tilt is a strong attractiveness cue.[5]
Photogrammetric studies of craniosynostosis surgery and of pageant winners report canthal tilt measurements.[3][6]
A 3D photogrammetry study in 145 dermatochalasis patients records canthal tilt by age and sex.[4]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, canthal tilt is discussed as a core eye-area metric and a frequent source of anxiety and advice threads.[8][9]

claims.claim: A positive canthal tilt is a key marker of male attractiveness.
claims.believers: Forum users treat positive tilt as part of the ideal eye area and compare faces by tilt.[10][9]
claims.experts: Tilt is a standard surgical measurement, and one 2007 paper examined it as an attractiveness cue, but published research has not established it as a main determinant of attractiveness.[5][4]

claims.claim: Mewing or tongue posture can raise canthal tilt by moving the upper jaw and cheeks.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster presented before-and-after photos after months of mewing and argued that pushing the maxilla supports the orbits and raises the tilt; replies were mixed and one said their own tilt did not change.[8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article notes that mewing lacks evidence of changing facial structure.[10]

claims.claim: Tilt cannot be changed without surgery.
claims.believers: Some users reply that exercises are ineffective and that only surgery or visual tricks like squinting and makeup can alter it.[8][9]
claims.experts: Surgical literature describes lateral canthal procedures chiefly for eyelid malposition, studied in retrospective series.[12]

claims.claim: A negative canthal tilt makes a man's outcomes hopeless.
claims.believers: Some threads describe negative tilt as an extreme handicap.[9]
claims.experts: No published study examines life outcomes as a function of canthal tilt.
